title: Functional Programming Best Practices
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of functional programming best practices and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply choosing the correct apply function in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Functional Programming Best Practices is part of Apply Functions and Functional Programming. Start with choosing the correct apply function and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Functions make behavior reusable; clear arguments, scope and return values make that behavior testable.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Functions make behavior reusable; clear arguments, scope and return values make that behavior testable. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Choosing the Correct Apply Function
items.text: Compare choosing the correct apply function using concrete trade-offs, assumptions and maintenance needs; state when each choice is appropriate.

items.title: Avoiding Accidental Simplification
items.text: Explain avoiding accidental simplification in the context of functional programming best practices, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Type-Safe Result Construction
items.text: Explain type-safe result construction in the context of functional programming best practices, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Readability vs. Cleverness
items.text: Explain readability vs. cleverness in the context of functional programming best practices, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Testing Functional Workflows
items.text: Turn testing functional workflows into a check with a clear condition, expected result and an example that should fail.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Call the function with typical, empty and invalid inputs, and inspect what it returns. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Functional Programming Best Practices
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 81: Functional Programming Best Practices
add_offset <- function(x, offset = 6) x + offset
add_offset(3)
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf does not provide an R runtime. This block is an inspectable reference example; execute it in a local R console or a reviewed R-aware environment. Static validation checks file structure, not R semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: Make inputs and return values explicit; also test an empty or invalid argument. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For functional programming best practices, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

content.task: Apply functional programming best practices to a small synthetic example. Start with choosing the correct apply function, predict the result, compare it with a local R run, test one edge or failure case, and document one limitation. For integrations or package-dependent topics, submit a safe verification plan rather than claiming the code ran.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
